units.title: Inventions
units.intro: Grammar: basic paragraphing II (developing paragraphs) and adverbs of frequency, including negative ones (seldom, rarely, hardly ever).

cards.title: Developing paragraphs
rule: Paragraphs can be developed by **examples**, **cause and effect** (*because, as a result*), **comparison and contrast** (*similarly, whereas, on the other hand*), or **process / time order** (*first, next, finally*).
Example: *The mobile phone has changed communication. **For example**, ... **As a result**, ...*

examples.text: The printing press spread knowledge. As a result, more people learned to read.
Whereas used to show a result.
examples.fix: Use as a result / therefore for results; whereas for contrast.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: Since the local library was renovated last year, the number of visitors ________ significantly.

steps.text: The subject is 'the number of visitors' (singular).
The sentence describes an action that started in the past (renovated last year) and continues to have relevance in the present, requiring the present perfect tense ($$\text{has/have} + \text{V}_3$$).
Students often see 'visitors' (plural) and choose 'have increased' (Option B).

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: The science teacher asked Dawit, 'Why ________ your assignment on time yesterday?'

steps.text: This is a direct question in the past simple tense.
Option A incorrectly combines 'didn't' with the past tense verb 'completed'.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The rare African manuscript ________ from the national archives before the guards noticed the broken window.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The sentence describes two past events: the manuscript being stolen and the guards noticing the broken window. The theft happened before the guards noticed it, requiring the past perfect passive voice ($$\text{had been} + \text{V}_3$$).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Each of the candidates who applied for the engineering position ________ a written test.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The subject of the sentence is 'Each' (singular), which always takes a singular verb and auxiliary ($$\text{Each} \rightarrow \text{singular verb}$$).

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**

cards.title: Adverbs of frequency
rule: From most to least: **always, usually, often, sometimes, seldom/rarely, hardly ever, never**.
Position: **before** the main verb (*I **often** use a computer*) but **after** be (*She is **always** late*) and after the first auxiliary (*I have **never** seen it*).
**seldom, rarely, hardly ever, never** already have a negative meaning, so do NOT add *not*: *I **hardly ever** watch TV* (not *I don’t hardly ever*).
cards.pattern: subject + adverb + main verb  ·  be + adverb

cards.title: Memory tip
body: **Seldom, rarely, hardly, never are already NO** — never add not.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Develop paragraphs with examples, cause and effect, comparison/contrast or process order. Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb, after be and after the first auxiliary; seldom, rarely, hardly ever and never are negative already.

glossary.meaning: Two negatives in one clause; incorrect in standard English.
